title: Area or perimeter? Covering versus going round
familyTitle: Choosing area or perimeter in a problem
skill: Decide whether a rectangle problem asks for area (covering) or perimeter (going round), then compute it.

knowledge: area of a rectangle as rows × squares in a row
perimeter as the total length of all sides

concept: Area is the space inside: how many unit squares cover the shape. For a rectangle, rows × squares in each row = length × width.
Perimeter is the distance round the edge: add all four sides, length + width + length + width.

visual.note: every square inside is shaded: covering

explanation.visualNote: Reuses the grid of squares (aearea / rows_of_squares); perimeter needs the outline emphasised, which the grid visual cannot do (visual gap).

workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular floor is 11 m long and 9 m wide. How many square tiles of side 1 m are needed to cover the floor?
familyExplainSteps: Covering needs the area: 9 rows of 11 squares = 99

workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular card is 10 cm long and 9 cm wide. How many centimetres of lace are needed to go once round the edge of the card?
lines: Going once round the edge: perimeter

hints: Is something covering the inside, or going round the edge?
Covering: count the squares inside, rows × squares in a row.
Is something covering the inside, or going round the edge?
Going round: add all four sides.

alternativeExplanation.title: Act it out
text: Tiling a floor: you lay squares all over it (area).
Fencing a garden: you walk round the edge (perimeter).

alternativeMethods.name: Perimeter as twice (length + width); area row by row

methodCredit: A correct final answer earns ANSWER credit only. Method credit needs a server-recorded verified working assessment. Checker status: none: no working contract.
diagnosticRule: A 'two-sides' answer (length + width) on the covering item and on the going-round item counts as two different errors (adding instead of multiplying; adding only half the sides), so the pair must not establish one misconception. A learner who multiplies on both items is right on the covering item and is suspected of area-for-perimeter only; one who adds all four sides on both is suspected of perimeter-for-area only.

misconceptions.note: conceptual: area and perimeter not distinguished

whatWentWrong: In "A rectangular card is 9 cm long and 6 cm wide. How many 1 cm squares of coloured paper are needed to cover the card?", one wrong answer is 30.
The perimeter was found, but covering the inside needs the area (how many squares fit inside).
Covering needs the squares INSIDE, not the length of the edge.
screens.counterCheck: Counter-check: draw 6 rows of 9 squares: there are 54 squares, not 30.

misconceptions.status: modelled (a single matching answer is a SUSPECTED error; established only under misconception-evidence@1: two matching answers)

whatWentWrong: In "A rectangular playground is 15 m long and 8 m wide. How many metres of rope are needed to go once round the playground?", one wrong answer is 120.
The area was found, but going round the edge needs the perimeter (the length all the way round).
Going round needs the length of the EDGE, not the squares inside.
solvedCorrectly: Going once round the edge: perimeter

misconceptions.status: modelled (a single matching answer is a SUSPECTED error; established only under misconception-evidence@1: two matching answers)
misconceptions.note: procedural: added one length and one width

whatWentWrong: In "A rectangular card is 12 cm long and 2 cm wide. How many centimetres of lace are needed to go once round the edge of the card?", one wrong answer is 14.
Only one length and one width were added (2 + 12). Going round passes all four sides.
Going round a rectangle passes all FOUR sides: two lengths and two widths.
screens.counterCheck: Counter-check: 12 + 2 = 14 is only half the way round.
solvedCorrectly: Going once round the edge: perimeter
